Engram Neuron Synapse Estimates

How Many Neurons & Synapses Are Involved in Recalling One Memory?

A single episodic memory is represented by a distributed engram: typically thousands to millions of neurons across hippocampus and neocortex, with millions to billions of synapses participating via modified weights. Recall often starts with a small cue-triggered subset of engram cells (hundreds–thousands) and rapidly recruits the wider network (pattern completion).

  • Cue / Partial Inputsensory/contextual triggers ~10^2 – 10^3 neurons
  • Hippocampal Engram CA3/DG/CA1 ensemble; pattern completion Engram fraction observed in rodents ≈ region of 10^5 neurons → 2×10^3 – 5×10^3 Synapses engaged: ~10^6–10^7
  • Cortical Spread / Distributed perceptual/semantic traces ~10^4 –1 0^6 neurons ~10^7–10^9 synapses
  • Full Recall (Reconstruction) Hippocampus coordinates pattern completion; cortex reinstates distributed content; amygdala/striatum contribute affect/habit - Total neurons involved: ~10^4 – 10^6

Total synapses participating: ~10^7–10^9
Numbers vary by species, region size, task complexity, and memory age (remote memories rely more on cortex).

Estimates integrate rodent engram fractions with known neuron/synapse counts and the complementary learning systems framework. They are order-of-magnitude guides, not precise tallies.

  • Engram fraction Rodent studies report ≈2–5% of neurons in a region tagged/necessary for a specific memory; recall can be driven by activating that subset.
  • Regional scale Hippocampal subfields in mice contain ~10^5 neurons; human regions are larger, implying more cells per memory.
  • Connectivity Typical neurons have 10^3–10^4 synapses, so thousands of engaged neurons imply ≥ millions of synapses.
  • Systems view Hippocampus rapidly indexes memories; neocortex stores distributed components and supports remote recall after consolidation.

References

  2. Engram overview & estimates: Josselyn & Tonegawa (2020), Science. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaw4325)
  3. Memory systems & consolidation: Frankland & Bontempi (2005), Nat. Rev. Neurosci.. https://www.nature.com/articles/nrn1647
  4. Complementary Learning Systems: McClelland, McNaughton & O’Reilly (1995), Psychological Review. https://stanford.edu/~jlmcc/papers/95-07.pdf

  6. Attractor dynamics & pattern completion: Rolls (2013), Front. Behav. Neurosci.. https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnbeh.2013.00133/full Numbers are synthesized from these sources and scaled as back‑of‑the‑envelope estimates; true counts vary widely by memory type, brain region, and individual differences.
